title: How Pachelbel's Canon got famous
hook: The wedding favourite was barely known until a 1968 recording.
peek: Johann Pachelbel wrote his Canon in D in the late 1600s, and then it slipped out of sight for centuries. A slow, lush 1968 recording by Jean-François Paillard helped turn it into the tune that now plays at countless weddings.
lede: Johann Pachelbel was a respected German organist of the 17th century who taught members of the Bach family. His Canon in D, written for three violins and a bass line, survived in a single manuscript copy and was not printed until 1919. Then in 1968 Jean-François Paillard's chamber orchestra recorded it at a slower, warmer pace, and the piece began its climb to fame.

bullets.opening: A canon over a ground bass
bullets.text: The bass plays the same eight notes 28 times. Above it, three violins play one long melody, each starting two bars after the last, like singers in a round.

Paillard's version added a richer, slower sound than the light Baroque style of earlier performances. It sold widely in the early 1970s, and the canon soon turned up in films, adverts and wedding processions.
The film Ordinary People used the canon as its main theme. That helped fix the piece as a symbol of calm and ceremony for a new audience.

The canon's repeating chords have been reused in countless pop songs. Maroon 5's 2019 hit Memories openly borrows the progression, and comedians have built whole routines around spotting it everywhere.
